claims.text: An approximately 100 nm ZrN interlayer can be deposited between a zirconium-alloy substrate and an elemental Cr coating using physical vapor deposition.
Proper surface pretreatment and optimized deposition will produce a dense and adherent ZrN interlayer.
The ZrN interlayer will inhibit Cr–Zr interdiffusion at approximately 320 °C.
The ZrN interlayer will inhibit Cr–Zr interdiffusion in steam at temperatures up to approximately 1200 °C for 1–2 hours.
Approximately 320 °C represents normal PWR primary-water operation for the proposed system.
Steam exposure up to approximately 1200 °C for 1–2 hours is an accident-relevant transient boundary.
A dense ZrN layer acts as a physical barrier to atomic diffusion between Cr and Zr.
The ZrN interlayer forms strong chemical bonds with both the zirconium-alloy substrate and the Cr coating.
ZrN has sufficiently low diffusivity and thermal stability to block migration of Cr and Zr atoms under the specified conditions.
Cr–Zr interdiffusion contributes to premature failure of elemental Cr coatings on zirconium-alloy substrates.
Optimized deposition will improve interlayer adhesion sufficiently to withstand cyclic thermal stresses.
Relative to Cr deposited directly on zirconium alloy, the ZrN-containing system will have a significantly lower Cr–Zr interdiffusion rate.
Reduced Cr–Zr interdiffusion will prolong coating integrity.
The ZrN-containing coating will sustain corrosion resistance during normal PWR-water operation better than the unmodified Cr-coated baseline.
The ZrN-containing coating will sustain corrosion resistance during accident-relevant high-temperature steam exposure better than the unmodified Cr-coated baseline.
An elemental Cr coating deposited directly on zirconium alloy undergoes accelerated interdiffusion at elevated temperature.
Long-term mechanical stability and adherence of the approximately 100 nm ZrN interlayer under cyclic thermal and mechanical stresses are not yet established.
Comparison of otherwise equivalent Cr-coated zirconium-alloy specimens with and without the ZrN interlayer can discriminate the intervention's effect.
TEM/EDS, adhesion testing, mechanical-integrity testing, and corrosion testing can be used to compare interdiffusion and coating integrity between the two specimen sets.
The hypothesis is falsified by no significant interdiffusion reduction, interlayer delamination or deterioration, or failure to improve corrosion resistance relative to the baseline.
